concepts.title: Addition
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: Adding means putting quantities together: 3 sweets + 4 sweets = 7 sweets. The column method lines up place values so ones add to ones, tens to tens, carrying groups of ten leftwards when a column overflows. Fluency here is not about speed for its own sake — it frees your working memory for harder ideas built on top.

concepts.lesson: 0.3 is 3/10; 0.07 is 7/100. Decimal place value extends the same left-right logic as whole numbers. Comparing decimals: line up place value — 0.09 < 0.1 even though 9 > 1. Multiplying shifts the point: 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.06 because tenths times tenths are hundredths.

concepts.title: Division
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: 12 ÷ 3 asks either 'how many groups of 3 fit in 12?' (4) or 'if 12 is shared into 3 equal parts, how big is each part?' (4). Long division splits the number by place value. Remainders matter: 13 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 1, which later becomes the fraction 3¼ and the decimal 3.25.

concepts.title: Fractions
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: A fraction a/b means a parts, each of size 1/b. The bottom number names the size of the part; the top counts them. 1/4 of a pizza is bigger than 1/8 because quarters are bigger slices. Equivalent fractions (1/2 = 3/6) multiply top and bottom by the same number — the value doesn't change because you're scaling both part-size and count equally.

misconceptions.name: Bigger denominator = bigger slice
misconceptions.pattern: Believes 1/8 > 1/4 because 8 > 4 — reading the denominator as a size, not a count of slices.

items.prompt: Work out 5/6 + 7/10. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
items.explanation: The denominators are different, so the fractions cannot be counted directly. The lowest common denominator of 6 and 10 is 30: 5/6 = 25/30 and 7/10 = 21/30. So the answer is (25 + 21)/30 = 23/15. Adding the bottoms (12/16) treats the denominator as a size to add rather than a count of equal parts — the bottom number says what the parts are, never how many.

concepts.title: Negative numbers
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: A negative is an amount below zero — temperatures, debt, depths. The rules that matter: subtracting a negative adds (5 − (−3) = 8), multiplying two negatives makes a positive ((−2) × (−3) = 6), and one negative makes a negative. Picture a number line: adding moves right, subtracting moves left.

concepts.title: Order of operations
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: Brackets, then Indices/Exponents, then Division and Multiplication left to right, then Addition and Subtraction left to right (BIDMAS/PEMDAS). 3 + 4 × 2 = 3 + 8 = 11, not 14 — multiplication always acts first. concepts.title: Place value
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: In the number 452, the digit 4 means 400, the 5 means 50 and the 2 means 2. Each step left multiplies a digit's value by ten, and each step right divides it by ten. This single idea is why we can write enormous numbers compactly, and it is the foundation of decimal numbers, estimation and standard form later on.

items.prompt: In the number 979, what is the VALUE of the ones digit?
items.explanation: In 979 the columns are worth 100, 10 and 1 from the left, so every digit is scaled by the column it sits in. The ones digit on its own is 9, but its VALUE is 9 — writing the digit instead of the value is the usual slip, and 90 would be one column further left.

concepts.title: Subtraction
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: Subtraction answers two questions: how much is left after taking away, and how far apart two numbers are. The column method borrows from the next place value when a digit cannot be reduced. A key early insight: subtraction is the inverse of addition, so you can always check an answer by adding back.

items.prompt: How far is the point (−4, 2) from the origin (0, 0)?

concepts.title: Fraction arithmetic
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: Add or subtract with a common denominator: 1/3 + 1/4 = 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12. Multiply straight across: 2/3 × 3/5 = 6/15 = 2/5. Divide by flipping the second fraction and multiplying: 2/3 ÷ 1/6 = 2/3 × 6/1 = 4. The flip works because dividing by 1/6 asks 'how many sixths fit?' — and there are 6 sixths in every whole.

misconceptions.name: Adds denominators

items.prompt: Work out 5/7 + 5/7. Give your answer as a decimal (2 d.p.).
items.explanation: Fractions can only be added once the pieces are the same size, so both are rewritten over the common denominator 49: 5/7 = 35/49 and 5/7 = 35/49. Adding the numerators then gives 70/49 = 1.43. Adding the tops and the bottoms (10/14) is the classic error, and it can even produce a fraction smaller than one of the originals — which a sum never is.

Adding the numerators then gives 19/15 = 1.27. concepts.title: Index laws
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: a³ means a × a × a. Multiplying powers with the same base adds the indices: a² × a³ = a⁵. Dividing subtracts them: a⁵ ÷ a² = a³. A power of zero gives 1 (a⁰ = 1) because dividing aⁿ by aⁿ must give 1. Negative indices flip into a fraction: a⁻² = 1/a². Fractional indices are roots: a^(1/2) = √a.

misconceptions.name: Misreads negative indices
misconceptions.pattern: Treats a⁻² as a negative number instead of 1/a².

items.prompt: Work out (4^2)².
items.explanation: A power raised to another power MULTIPLIES the indices, because the factors are themselves repeated: (4^2)² means 4^2 written twice, which is 2 + 2 = 4 factors of 4. So the value is 4^4 = 256. Adding the indices instead (4^4 = 256) is the rule for multiplying powers, not for raising one to a power, and doubling the value of 4^2 (32) is not a power at all.

concepts.title: Linear equations
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: Solve 3x + 5 = 20 by undoing operations in reverse order: subtract 5 (3x = 15), divide by 3 (x = 5). Whatever you do to one side, do to the other — the equation is a balance. Two-step, brackets, unknowns on both sides (5x = 2x + 9) all reduce to the same discipline.

misconceptions.name: Breaks the balance when solving
misconceptions.pattern: Adds to one side only: 3x + 5 = 20 becomes 3x = 25.

items.prompt: Solve 3(x + 2) = 30.
items.explanation: The whole bracket is multiplied by 3, so dividing both sides by 3 undoes it and leaves x + 2 = 10; subtracting 2 then gives x = 8. Expanding first reaches the same place, because 3x + 6 = 30. Dividing by 5 instead (6) divides by a number that is not what multiplies the bracket.

concepts.title: Percentages
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: Percent means 'per hundred': 45% = 45/100 = 0.45. Percentage of an amount: 15% of 60 = 0.15 × 60 = 9. Percentage change = (new − old)/old × 100. A classic trap: a 20% rise then a 20% fall does not return to the start — 100 → 120 → 96 — because the second percentage acts on a different base.

items.explanation: A rise of 10% is one multiplication by 1.1, because the new price is the whole original price plus the extra part of it. So 80 × 1.1 = 88. Adding 10 to the price (90) treats the percentage as 10 pounds, and 8 is only the increase, not the new price.

items.prompt: A price of 120 rises by 25%. What is the new price?
items.explanation: A rise of 25% is one multiplication by 1.25, because the new price is the whole original price plus the extra part of it. So 120 × 1.25 = 150. Adding 25 to the price (145) treats the percentage as 25 pounds, and 30 is only the increase, not the new price.

items.prompt: A price of $100 rises by 25%, then falls by 25%. What is the final price (in $)?
items.explanation: The rise takes 100 to 125, because 25% of 100 is 25. The fall then acts on the new price, 125, not on the original: 25% of 125 is 31.25, so the final price is 93.75. The fall is larger in money than the rise because the base has grown, which is why the final price is below 100; taking 25% off the original again would wrongly return 100.

items.prompt: A price of 80 falls by 25%. What is the new price?
items.explanation: A fall of 25% leaves 75% of the price, so the whole calculation is one multiplication by 0.75: 80 × 0.75 = 60. Subtracting 25 from the price treats the percentage as 25 pounds, and multiplying by 1.25 applies a rise instead of a cut.

items.prompt: A price rises by 50% and then falls by 40%. What is the overall percentage change?
items.explanation: Work with multipliers, never added percentages: a 50% rise is ×1.5 and a 40% fall is ×0.6. Multiplying: ×0.9, an overall change of −10%. The fall acts on the RAISED price — a different base — which is why 50% up and 40% down do not cancel.

concepts.title: Expanding & factorising
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: Expand: (x + 3)(x + 2) = x² + 5x + 6 — every term meets every term. Factorising reverses it: x² + 5x + 6 seeks two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5: (x + 2)(x + 3). The difference of two squares is a shortcut: x² − 9 = (x + 3)(x − 3). These skills are the grammar of every later algebra topic.

misconceptions.name: Sign error when expanding
misconceptions.pattern: (x − 3)(x + 2) becomes x² + 5x − 6 — the minus doesn't distribute.

items.prompt: Expand (x + 5)(x + 8). The result is x² + bx + c. What is the value of b?
items.explanation: Expanding means every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second, and the two x terms then combine: x × x gives x², 5x and 8x add to 13x, and the constants multiply to 40. So b, the coefficient of x, is 13. Multiplying instead of adding (40) gives c, the constant term, and 14 counts one of the x terms twice.

items.prompt: Expand and simplify (x + 4)(x + 2).
items.explanation: Multiply every term in the first bracket by every term in the second: x × x = x², x × 2 = 2x, 4 × x = 4x, and 4 × 2 = 8. The two x-terms are like terms, so 2x + 4x = 6x, giving x² + 6x + 8. The usual slip is dropping the 8 term or losing its sign, which is why every term must carry its sign.

items.prompt: Expand (x + 9)(x + 8). The result is x² + bx + c. What is the value of b?
items.explanation: Expanding means every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second, and the two x terms then combine: x × x gives x², 9x and 8x add to 17x, and the constants multiply to 72. So b, the coefficient of x, is 17. Multiplying instead of adding (72) gives c, the constant term, and 18 counts one of the x terms twice.

items.prompt: Expand and simplify (x + -5)(x + 1).
items.explanation: Multiply every term in the first bracket by every term in the second: x × x = x², x × 1 = 1x, -5 × x = -5x, and -5 × 1 = -5. The two x-terms are like terms, so 1x + -5x = -4x, giving x² − 4x − 5. The usual slip is dropping the -5 term or losing its sign, which is why every term must carry its sign.

items.prompt: Expand and simplify (x + 5)(x + 1).
items.explanation: Multiply every term in the first bracket by every term in the second: x × x = x², x × 1 = 1x, 5 × x = 5x, and 5 × 1 = 5. The two x-terms are like terms, so 1x + 5x = 6x, giving x² + 6x + 5. The usual slip is dropping the 5 term or losing its sign, which is why every term must carry its sign.

items.prompt: Expand (x + 8)(x + 9). The result is x² + bx + c. What is the value of b?
items.explanation: Expanding means every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second, and the two x terms then combine: x × x gives x², 8x and 9x add to 17x, and the constants multiply to 72. So b, the coefficient of x, is 17. Multiplying instead of adding (72) gives c, the constant term, and 18 counts one of the x terms twice.

items.prompt: Expand (2x + 6)(x + 4). The result is 2x² + bx + c. What is the value of b?
items.explanation: The x term has two sources, because either term of the first bracket can meet the x in the second: 2x × 4 = 8x, and 6 × x = 6x. Adding those gives 14x, so b = 14. The other pairing, 2x with 6, is a term in x², and 6 × 4 = 24 is the constant.

items.prompt: The area of a rectangle is (x² + 13x + 42) cm² and its width is (x + 6) cm. What is its length, in terms of x?
items.explanation: Area = width × length, so length = area ÷ width. Factorise first: x² + 13x + 42 = (x + 6)(x + 7), because 6 × 7 = 42 and 6 + 7 = 13. Dividing by the width (x + 6) leaves (x + 7) cm. The two numbers must MULTIPLY to the constant and ADD to the coefficient of x — a sign slip breaks one of those conditions, and the wrong factors are what the distractors are made of.

items.prompt: The area of a rectangle is (x² + 8x + 15) cm² and its width is (x + 5) cm. What is its length, in terms of x?
items.explanation: Area = width × length, so length = area ÷ width. Factorise first: x² + 8x + 15 = (x + 5)(x + 3), because 5 × 3 = 15 and 5 + 3 = 8. Dividing by the width (x + 5) leaves (x + 3) cm. The two numbers must MULTIPLY to the constant and ADD to the coefficient of x — a sign slip breaks one of those conditions, and the wrong factors are what the distractors are made of.

items.prompt: The area of a rectangle is (x² + 9x + 18) cm² and its width is (x + 6) cm. What is its length, in terms of x?

The two numbers must MULTIPLY to the constant and ADD to the coefficient of x — a sign slip breaks one of those conditions, and the wrong factors are what the distractors are made of.

items.prompt:
Expand and simplify (2x + 7)(4x − 4).

What is the coefficient of x in the expansion?
items.explanation: The x-term is the sum of the two CROSS products: the outer pair 2x × -4 = -8x, and the inner pair 7 × 4x = 28x. Adding them: -8 + 28 → the coefficient is 20. Stopping at -8 forgets the inner pair, and 28 forgets the outer one — the two halves of the same step. 8 is the coefficient of x², and -28 is the constant.

items.prompt: The area of a rectangle is (x² + 7x + 12) cm² and its width is (x + 3) cm. What is its length, in terms of x?
items.explanation: Area = width × length, so length = area ÷ width. Factorise first: x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4), because 3 × 4 = 12 and 3 + 4 = 7. Dividing by the width (x + 3) leaves (x + 4) cm. The two numbers must MULTIPLY to the constant and ADD to the coefficient of x — a sign slip breaks one of those conditions, and the wrong factors are what the distractors are made of.

concepts.title: Straight line graphs
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: In y = mx + c, m is the gradient (rise over run — how much y grows per unit of x) and c is where the line crosses the y-axis. Parallel lines share m; perpendicular lines multiply to −1. From two points, m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Every real-world rate — speed, cost per item, fuel use — is a gradient.

misconceptions.name: Gradient upside-down or sign-flipped
misconceptions.pattern: Computes run over rise, or drops the minus on a downhill line.

items.prompt: A line has equation y = 4x + 5. What is y when x = 6?
items.explanation: The equation gives y in terms of x, so finding y when x is 6 means putting 6 wherever x appears. 4 × 6 = 24, and then adding 5 gives 29. Dropping the 5 altogether (24) forgets that the line does not pass through the origin, and getting its sign the other way round (19) puts the intercept on the wrong side.

items.prompt:
A straight line passes through (4, -30) and (5, -33).

Work out the coordinates of the point where the line crosses the x-axis.
items.explanation: Three steps, and the third is the one asked for. Gradient: (-33 − -30) ÷ (5 − 4) = -3 ÷ 1 = -3. Intercept: at (4, -30), -30 = -3 × 4 + c, so c = -18. Root: the line crosses the x-axis where y = 0, so 0 = -3x − 18, giving x = -6. The point is (-6, 0). Answering (0, -18) is where the line crosses the Y-axis — the same shape of question about the other axis.

items.prompt:
A straight line passes through (4, 0) and (5, -3).

Work out the coordinates of the point where the line crosses the x-axis.
items.explanation: Three steps, and the third is the one asked for. Gradient: (-3 − 0) ÷ (5 − 4) = -3 ÷ 1 = -3. Intercept: at (4, 0), 0 = -3 × 4 + c, so c = 12. Root: the line crosses the x-axis where y = 0, so 0 = -3x + 12, giving x = 4. The point is (4, 0). Answering (0, 12) is where the line crosses the Y-axis — the same shape of question about the other axis.

items.prompt: A water tank holds 60 litres. Water is added at a steady 2 litres per minute. A graph of volume (y litres) against time (x minutes) is a straight line. How much water is in the tank after 14 minutes?
items.explanation: The line is y = 2x + 60: the gradient 2 is the change per minute and 60 is the volume at x = 0, the intercept. After 14 minutes: 2 × 14 + 60 = 88 litres. Answering 28 reports the water ADDED rather than the water in the tank — the intercept dropped because it was never written down.

concepts.title: Completing the square
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4: halve the x coefficient, square it, adjust. This form exposes the vertex (−3, −4) instantly, shows the minimum/maximum value, and solves equations by isolating a perfect square. It is also how the quadratic formula is derived — completing the square on the general equation.

misconceptions.name: Completing the square: forgets the constant
misconceptions.pattern: x² + 6x + 5 becomes (x + 3)² without subtracting the added 9.

items.prompt: Express x² + 10x + 21 in the form (x + p)² + q, and hence state the minimum value of the expression and the value of x at which it occurs.
items.explanation: Half the coefficient of x is 5, so the square is (x + 5)² = x² + 10x + 25; the expression has 21 there instead, so it is (x + 5)² − 4 = (x + 5)² − 4. A square is never negative, so the SMALLEST the expression gets is when (x + 5)² = 0 — that is x = -5, and the minimum value is -4. The sign of p is the slip: it is −h in the bracket, so the minimum sits at the opposite sign, -5.

items.prompt: What is the minimum value of y = x² − 10x + 30?
items.explanation: Complete the square: half of −10 is −5, and (x − 5)² expands to x² − 10x + 25. The expression is therefore (x − 5)² + 5; a square is never negative, so the smallest value is 5, reached when x = 5. Reading the constant 30 as the minimum forgets to subtract the 25 that completing the square introduced, and -5 is the x-value where the minimum occurs, not the minimum itself.

items.prompt: What is the minimum value of y = x² − 14x + 54?
items.explanation: Complete the square: half of −14 is −7, and (x − 7)² expands to x² − 14x + 49. The expression is therefore (x − 7)² + 5; a square is never negative, so the smallest value is 5, reached when x = 7. Reading the constant 54 as the minimum forgets to subtract the 49 that completing the square introduced, and -7 is the x-value where the minimum occurs, not the minimum itself.

items.prompt: What is the minimum value of y = x² − 8x + 23?
items.explanation: Complete the square: half of −8 is −4, and (x − 4)² expands to x² − 8x + 16. The expression is therefore (x − 4)² + 7; a square is never negative, so the smallest value is 7, reached when x = 4. Reading the constant 23 as the minimum forgets to subtract the 16 that completing the square introduced, and -4 is the x-value where the minimum occurs, not the minimum itself.

items.prompt: Express x² + 6x + 3 in the form (x + p)² + q, and hence state the minimum value of the expression and the value of x at which it occurs.
items.explanation: Half the coefficient of x is 3, so the square is (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9; the expression has 3 there instead, so it is (x + 3)² − 6 = (x + 3)² − 6. A square is never negative, so the SMALLEST the expression gets is when (x + 3)² = 0 — that is x = -3, and the minimum value is -6. The sign of p is the slip: it is −h in the bracket, so the minimum sits at the opposite sign, -3.

items.prompt: Express x² + 6x + 1 in the form (x + p)² + q, and hence state the minimum value of the expression and the value of x at which it occurs.
items.explanation: Half the coefficient of x is 3, so the square is (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9; the expression has 1 there instead, so it is (x + 3)² − 8 = (x + 3)² − 8. A square is never negative, so the SMALLEST the expression gets is when (x + 3)² = 0 — that is x = -3, and the minimum value is -8. The sign of p is the slip: it is −h in the bracket, so the minimum sits at the opposite sign, -3.

concepts.title: Quadratic equations
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: Quadratics can have two, one, or no real solutions — visible as where the parabola cuts the x-axis. Solve by factorising (x² − 5x + 6 = 0 → (x−2)(x−3) = 0 → x = 2 or 3), by completing the square, or by the quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. The discriminant b² − 4ac tells you how many solutions exist before you solve.

misconceptions.name: Loses a root when solving quadratics
misconceptions.pattern: Divides by x instead of factorising, or takes only one ± branch.

items.prompt: Solve x² − 9x + 18 = 0. Give the smaller root.
items.explanation: The two numbers must multiply to 18 and add to 9; 3 and 6 do both, so the equation factorises as (x − 3)(x − 6) = 0. A product is zero only when one bracket is zero, so x = 3 or x = 6. The question asks for the smaller root, 3; 6 is the other root and 9 is their sum, not a root at all.

items.prompt: Solve x² − 8x + 15 = 0. Give the smaller root.
items.explanation: The two numbers must multiply to 15 and add to 8; 5 and 3 do both, so the equation factorises as (x − 5)(x − 3) = 0. A product is zero only when one bracket is zero, so x = 5 or x = 3. The question asks for the smaller root, 3; 5 is the other root and 8 is their sum, not a root at all.

items.prompt: Solve x² − 6x + 5 = 0. Give the smaller root.
items.explanation: The two numbers must multiply to 5 and add to 6; 5 and 1 do both, so the equation factorises as (x − 5)(x − 1) = 0. A product is zero only when one bracket is zero, so x = 5 or x = 1. The question asks for the smaller root, 1; 5 is the other root and 6 is their sum, not a root at all.

items.prompt: Solve x² − 9x + 20 = 0. Give the smaller root.
items.explanation: The two numbers must multiply to 20 and add to 9; 4 and 5 do both, so the equation factorises as (x − 4)(x − 5) = 0. A product is zero only when one bracket is zero, so x = 4 or x = 5. The question asks for the smaller root, 4; 5 is the other root and 9 is their sum, not a root at all.

items.prompt: Solve x² − 6x + 8 = 0. Give the smaller root.
items.explanation: The two numbers must multiply to 8 and add to 6; 2 and 4 do both, so the equation factorises as (x − 2)(x − 4) = 0. A product is zero only when one bracket is zero, so x = 2 or x = 4. The question asks for the smaller root, 2; 4 is the other root and 6 is their sum, not a root at all.

items.prompt: The graph of y = x² − 5x + 6 crosses the x-axis at two points. What are the x-coordinates of those points?
items.explanation: The crossings are where y = 0, so solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0 by factorising: two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to -5 are 3 and 2, giving (x − 3)(x − 2) = 0. A product is zero when either factor is zero, so x = 2 OR x = 3 — reporting one root throws away half the answer.

items.prompt: The graph of y = x² + x − 30 crosses the x-axis at two points. What are the x-coordinates of those points?
items.explanation: The crossings are where y = 0, so solve x² + 1x − 30 = 0 by factorising: two numbers that multiply to -30 and add to 1 are 5 and -6, giving (x − 5)(x + 6) = 0. A product is zero when either factor is zero, so x = -6 OR x = 5 — reporting one root throws away half the answer.

items.prompt: The equation x² + 10x + c = 0 has exactly one solution. What is c?
items.explanation: A quadratic has exactly one solution when its two roots coincide, which happens when the expression is a perfect square. Half of the x-coefficient is 5, so the square is (x + 5)² = x² + 10x + 25; matching the constant gives c = 25. Answering 5 takes half the coefficient as the constant, and 26 or 24 changes the square so it no longer has one repeated root.

items.prompt: The graph of y = x² − x − 20 crosses the x-axis at two points. What are the x-coordinates of those points?
items.explanation: The crossings are where y = 0, so solve x² − 1x − 20 = 0 by factorising: two numbers that multiply to -20 and add to -1 are -4 and 5, giving (x + 4)(x − 5) = 0. A product is zero when either factor is zero, so x = -4 OR x = 5 — reporting one root throws away half the answer.

items.prompt: The graph of y = x² − 6x + 8 crosses the x-axis at two points. What are the x-coordinates of those points?
items.explanation: The crossings are where y = 0, so solve x² − 6x + 8 = 0 by factorising: two numbers that multiply to 8 and add to -6 are 4 and 2, giving (x − 4)(x − 2) = 0. A product is zero when either factor is zero, so x = 2 OR x = 4 — reporting one root throws away half the answer.

items.prompt: The graph of y = x² + x − 2 crosses the x-axis at two points. What are the x-coordinates of those points?
items.explanation: The crossings are where y = 0, so solve x² + 1x − 2 = 0 by factorising: two numbers that multiply to -2 and add to 1 are 1 and -2, giving (x − 1)(x + 2) = 0. A product is zero when either factor is zero, so x = -2 OR x = 1 — reporting one root throws away half the answer.

concepts.title: Surds
concepts.subject: maths
concepts.lesson: √2 cannot be written exactly as a fraction — its decimal never repeats. A surd is an exact root like √2, √3, √5. Simplify using √(ab) = √a × √b: √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2. Rationalise denominators by multiplying top and bottom by the surd (or its conjugate for expressions like 1/(1+√2)). Surds keep answers exact where decimals only approximate.

items.prompt: Write √7 + √112 in the form k√7. What is k?
items.explanation: Simplify each surd before adding: √7 = √(1 × 7) = 1√7, and √112 = √(16 × 7) = 4√7. The two terms now have the same radical, so they are like terms and their coefficients add: 1 + 4 = 5. Multiplying the coefficients (4) is the rule for √a × √b, not for a sum, and leaving them unsimplified hides that the radicals match.
